To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the two members of the class A bHLh family ME1a and 2 are differently expressed and bind to different DNA sequences in the adult brain and that their activity can be regulated by Id2.
ME1a/ME2 heterodimers and Id2 homodimers bind to different target genes, suggesting a unique role for ME1a and/or ME2 during neurogenesis and neuronal plasticity in the adult brain.

ME1a is expressed in the developing brain and in areas of the mature brain where neuronal plastic events take place, and that it forms heterodimers and homodimers with ME2, which are differentially involved during neurogenesis and neuronal plasticity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of differences in expression, DNA-binding specificity and transcriptional activity of two class A bHHL proteins, ME1a and 2, in differentiating neuronal cell lines.
the elucidation of ME1a- and ME2-specific roles, in particular, during neuronal plasticity.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanism by which ME1a and/or ME2 regulate neuronal plasticity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ME1a is expressed in areas of the brain where neuronal plastic occurs, and ME2 is involved in neuronal development.
ME1a is a neuronal-specific class A bHLHe protein that is involved in the control and regulation of neuronal plasticity and that Id2 acts as a repressor of ME1a transcriptional activity.
both ME1a and 2 are involved in neuronal development and plasticity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
differential expression and distinct DNA binding specificity of ME1 and ME2 suggest that they have unique roles in neuronal differentiation and plasticity.
ME1a/ME2 are not redundant, and their differential expression and distinct DNA binding specificity may be important for the control of neuronal plasticity.
ME1a, ME2 and Id2 may be involved in the regulation of neuronal plasticity and that their expression and activity are regulated by neuronal stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ME1a/ME2 and Id2 are likely to have a role in the modulation of gene expression in neuronal cells during differentiation.
ME1a, ME2, and Id2 are differentially involved in neuronal plasticity.
the differential expression of ME1a versus ME2 and their distinct DNA-binding specificities suggest a unique role for these proteins during differentiation and neuronal cell plasticity.
